aoi.description: Select the area you want to analyse. All subsequent steps will be clipped to this boundary.

variables.description: Add input variables for the risk model.
variables.info_md:
Source variables are the input layers the risk model is built from. Add them from two sources:

- **predefined** — ready-made layers fetched from [Google Earth Engine](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets) and clipped to your AOI. Each comes from a published global dataset: elevation and slope (NASA SRTM), forest cover (Hansen Global Forest Change or JRC Tropical Moist Forest), protected areas (WDPA), rivers and roads (OpenStreetMap), towns (JRC GHSL) and subjurisdictions (FAO GAUL). Select one in the Add Variable dialog to see exactly how it is generated and where the data comes from.
- **custom** — your own data: a local GeoTIFF raster, a local vector file (GeoJSON/GPKG/SHP — rasterized during harmonization), or any GEE image asset you have access to.

Temporal variables (e.g. forest cover) carry a year, so the same layer can be added for several years. All layers are brought onto one common grid in the Harmonization step.

GEE-backed variables show a **cloud** chip until they are exported from Earth Engine and saved as local GeoTIFFs — use **Download layers** (or a row's cloud-download button) to materialize them.

process.description: Set the reference raster + projection, then harmonize all variables onto its grid.
process.info_md:
This step brings every source variable onto one common analysis grid:

1. **Reference & projection** — pick one raster as the **reference raster**: it defines the grid (CRS, pixel size and extent) every other layer is aligned to. Choose the layer whose spatial detail matters most — typically the forest-cover layer the deforestation target is derived from. Use a projected CRS in metres; the ⌖ icon in the EPSG field suggests the UTM zone of the layer.
2. **Run harmonization** — missing GEE layers are downloaded, every raster is reprojected and resampled onto the reference grid, and vector layers are rasterized onto it. Afterwards all harmonized layers overlap pixel-by-pixel (same CRS, resolution and extent), which model training and prediction require — these are the harmonized variables used by the next steps.

GEE-backed layers are downloaded in the Variables step; any still pending are downloaded automatically when harmonization runs. Re-run harmonization whenever you add or change source variables.

postprocess.description: Derive new variables from the harmonized layers: change detection (loss/gain) and edge/distance transforms.
postprocess.output_preview_invalid: Select valid inputs to see the output name.
postprocess.info_md:
This step derives new model inputs from the harmonized layers:

- **Change detection (loss / gain)** — compares two presence masks of the same phenomenon at two years and outputs a change mask (1 = event, 0 = stable, 255 = nodata). *loss* marks pixels present at the start but absent at the end (e.g. deforestation between two forest-cover years — the usual model target); *gain* marks the reverse (e.g. regrowth).
- **edge** — for each pixel *inside* a binary mask (value 1), the distance in metres to the mask's edge. Applied to a forest mask it gives distance-to-forest-edge, a key deforestation predictor.
- **dist** — for each pixel *outside* the mask, the distance in metres to the nearest mask pixel. Applied to roads, rivers or towns it gives distance-to-road / river / town.

Both transforms expect a binary (0/1) mask and produce a continuous raster. Results appear in the derived-variables list below and can be used as dataset features (the Dataset step).
postprocess.change_help_text: Pick two presence masks (1 = present, 0 = absent) of the same phenomenon at two different years — same or different sources. Output: 1 = event, 0 = stable, 255 = nodata.

postprocess.op_hint_gain: 1 where absent at start but present at the end (e.g. regrowth).
postprocess.op_hint_edge: Distance to the mask edge, inside the mask (e.g. distance to forest edge).
postprocess.op_hint_dist: Distance to the nearest mask pixel, outside it (e.g. distance to roads).

dataset.description: Bundle the layers a model learns from: one target (what to predict) and the features (the predictors).
dataset.info_md:
A dataset names the layers a model trains and predicts on:

- **Target** — the variable the model learns to predict: a binary event mask where **1 = event** and 0 = no event. Typically a deforestation *loss* layer generated in the Derived layers step from two forest-cover years.
- **Features** — the explanatory layers the model relates to the target: altitude, slope, distance to forest edge / roads / rivers / towns, protected areas, etc.
- **Year** — when the target or features are temporal (one layer per year), the year selects which annual layer each variable contributes.

Registering validates that every layer exists on disk and shares the common grid from the Harmonization step. Create separate datasets for calibration and validation periods so you can train on one and evaluate on the other.

sampling.description: Draw a persistent, named sample from a raster variable. Samples are selectable in the Train step and can be added to the map.
sampling.info_md:
A sample is a saved set of point locations drawn from the pixels of a raster variable; models later extract their training data at these points (the Train step). Sample types:

- **random** — points drawn uniformly at random among valid pixels.
- **stratified** — the raster's values define classes (strata; e.g. 0/1 of a deforestation mask) and points are drawn per class following the allocation rule: *equal* (total split evenly across classes), *proportional* (split by class pixel count), or *deforisk* (the requested count drawn from **each** class, as in forestatrisk).
- **systematic** — points on a regular grid, defined either by a total count or by the distance between points.

An optional mask restricts sampling to pixels where the mask is non-zero (e.g. forest at period start). The seed makes the draw reproducible.

evaluation.description: Score prediction maps against one chosen truth so maps from different datasets are comparable. Each saved run appears below — click it to view its table.
evaluation.info_md:
Each evaluation scores one or more prediction maps against a single user-chosen **truth**, so maps trained on different datasets can be compared on equal terms.

The truth is defined by three inputs:

- **Truth — observed deforestation** — the raster of deforestation that actually happened during the validation period.
- **Forest at period start** — the forest-cover raster at the start of that period.
- **Interval (years)** — the period length (pre-filled from the truth layer's name when possible).

For each selected map the area is aggregated into square cells of the chosen **cell size(s)** (in pixels) and the predicted deforestation rate is compared with the observed one in every cell. Accuracy indices:

- **MedAE** — median absolute error
- **R²** — coefficient of determination
- **RMSE** — root mean squared error
- **wRMSE** — RMSE weighted by each cell's forest area

Leave the map selection empty to evaluate every registered prediction. **Recompute defrate** rebuilds the observed rates instead of reusing cached ones. Each run is saved with the project and listed in this tab; open a row to view its full table.

stats.icar_mcmc_info_md:
This model cannot calculate its coefficients with a closed formula. Instead it approximates them by sampling (MCMC): a long random walk through plausible parameter values, spending more time at values that fit the data and the model's priors; the table above summarises where it went. These two numbers check for warning signs that the sampling cannot be trusted — they can reveal problems, but cannot prove the sampler explored everything.

**R-hat — did the sampling settle?** The recorded walk is split in half and the halves are compared. If sampling became stable, the values in the two halves have similar distributions and R-hat is close to 1.0. Values above ~1.1 mean the halves clearly differ — usually because the walk was still drifting when it stopped, so the estimate partly depends on where it happened to be.

**Effective sample size — how many independent looks?** Consecutive samples are nearly identical, like frames of a slowly panning video. ESS estimates how many independent samples would carry about the same information. Below roughly 100, the endpoints of the 95% intervals carry substantial simulation error — a warning threshold, not a guarantee either way.

**Why a note often appears for the spatial effect (Vrho).** Vrho — the variance that governs how large the spatial neighbourhood effect can be — moves very slowly in this sampler at affordable iteration counts. On its own that does not invalidate the coefficient table (the warning above only triggers on the coefficients themselves); it mainly means Vrho's interval endpoints are imprecise and could shift in a longer run.

---

**Technical details.** Diagnostics are computed on the single retained chain, after burn-in and thinning (thinning limits stored draws; it does not itself improve convergence). R-hat is the split R-hat of Gelman–Rubin with m = 2 half-chains: sqrt(var+/W), where W is the mean within-half variance and var+ adds the between-half component. It reacts to differences between the halves — trends above all — but a single chain can never rule out modes it simply never visited. ESS is N / (1 + 2 Σ ρτ), with N the retained draws and the autocorrelation sum truncated by Geyer's initial-positive-sequence rule (consecutive autocorrelations are summed in pairs; the sum stops at the first non-positive pair); ESS is itself an estimate and gets unreliable on short, highly autocorrelated chains. Warning thresholds: R-hat > 1.1 (a permissive practical cut; modern guidance prefers rank-normalised split R-hat < 1.01, a stricter statistic than the one computed here) or ESS < 100. Clean values are necessary, not sufficient, evidence of convergence. First remedy: retrain with more MCMC iterations and re-check — persistent problems may not be solved by run length alone.
